column2: He should always tend the fire, and perform the offering to beings before eating; for otherwise, Madhusudana, the gods are left unsatisfied.
Every day he should perform the shraddha, with food or with water, or even with milk, roots and fruits, offering delight to the ancestors.
From the cooked food he should make the Vaishvadeva offering into the fire according to rule: to Agni and Soma, to the Vishvedevas, and then to Dhanvantari.
Then, with what remains of that food, he should feed guests as well. First honour, O great king, and only then does he gratify men.
Because he stays but a short time, he is called a guest (atithi).
To the teacher, the father, the friend, the trusted kinsman and the guest, he should always declare, "This is what I have in my house."
Whatever they say, he should do; such is the ordained dharma. A householder, O Krishna, should always eat only what remains after others.
He should honour a king, a priest, a snataka, a teacher and a father-in-law with the madhuparka when they have stayed a full year.
For dogs, for outcastes and for birds he should scatter food on the ground; this is called the Vaishvadeva, enjoined at dusk and at dawn.
One who without envy practises these householder duties attains great prosperity here and, after death, is honoured in heaven.
[Bhishma] Having heard these words of the Earth, the mighty Vasudeva acted so at all times; you too should act in the same way.
Thus, O lord of men, if you keep this householder's dharma in mind, you will win fame in this world and attain heaven after death.
[Bhishma] On this too they cite an ancient tale: the dialogue between the lord of creatures Manu and Suvarna, O Bharata.
There was an ascetic named Suvarna, golden in hue, and so he became widely known as Suvarna.
He was endowed with good family, conduct and virtues, and had reached the height of Vedic study; by his own qualities he surpassed many born in his own line.
Once the brahmin saw Manu and approached him, and there the two exchanged greetings and inquiries after each other's welfare.
Then those two, whose resolves were fulfilled, sat down together on a delightful flat rock on Meru, the golden mountain.
There they told many kinds of tales about brahmin sages, gods, daityas and the great souls of old.
Suvarna said to the lord Manu Svayambhuva: "For the good of all beings, you should answer my question.
O lord of creatures, the gods are worshipped with flowers (sumanas). What are these, how did they come to be, and what is the fruit of offering them? Tell me."
Nectar gives delight to the mind and at once gives nourishment; poison, by its smell, sharply afflicts the mind everywhere.
Know nectar to be auspicious and great poison inauspicious. All plants are nectar; poison is fiery energy born of fire.
Because they gladden the mind and also bring prosperity, they are called "sumanas" by men of good deeds.
The pure man who gives flowers to the gods is so called because the gods are pleased by them.
O lord, whatever god flowers are offered to for the sake of good fortune, that god is pleased with him by them, O lord of the daityas.
Know that plants are of separate kinds: fierce, gentle and radiant, many of great potency and many in form.
Learn from me about trees fit for sacrifice and those not fit, and about garlands that are demonic and those that benefit the gods.
Some are dear to rakshasas, to gods, to yakshas, to ancestors, and to humans, and others to lovers, each in its order.
Some grow wild, some are village plants, some are cultivated and sown, some grow on mountains; some are thornless, some thorny, endowed with scent, form and flavour.
Scent from flowers is held to be of two kinds, pleasant and unpleasant. One should understand flowers of pleasant scent to be the gods'.
Flowers of thornless trees, mostly white in colour, are always dear to the gods, O lord.
Water-born garlands, lotuses and the like, the wise man should give to gandharvas, nagas and yakshas.
Plants with red flowers, bitter and thorny, are shown in the Atharvan texts for the sorcery against enemies.
Plants sharp in potency, hard to handle, thorny, mostly red or black in colour, are to be offered to fierce beings.
Those that delight the mind and heart, are sweet when pressed, and are lovely in form are held to be the flowers of men, O lord.
Not those born in cremation grounds or at temples; he should bring them for rites of prosperity, at weddings and in private.
Gentle flowers growing on mountain slopes he should offer to the gods, sprinkled and consecrated, in due manner as tradition says.
The gods are pleased by scent, yakshas and rakshasas by sight, nagas by enjoyment, and men by all three.
They at once please the gods, and, pleased, the gods grant to mortals fulfilment of their resolves and the desires of their hearts.
The gods, honoured, always gratify, and honour in return; but when slighted and cast aside they burn up base men.
Next I shall tell the fruit in the rule of giving incense. Learn of incenses, the good and the bad, of many kinds.
Resinous, sarala, and artificial are the three; the scent may be pleasing or not. Hear that from me in detail.
Among resins, sallaki is to be avoided, though dear to the gods; guggulu is the best of all, so it is settled.
Aguru is best for the sages, for yakshas, rakshasas and nagas; for daityas the sallaki-born, and what is like it, is desired.
Then, O king, by scents of sarja resin and the like, of woods, mixed with syrup and sour gruel, incense is prescribed for men.
It is held to give instant satisfaction to gods, danavas and spirits; others, meant for pleasure, are held to be for men.
The very qualities said to be the reasons in giving flowers should be understood to apply also to incense; they increase delight.
I shall now tell the supreme fruit in giving lamps: how, by whom, when, and of what sort they should be given.
Light, radiance and brightness are described as rising upward; so in giving lights one increases the radiance of men.
Blindness, darkness, deep gloom, the southern course and the northern course: from these, the gift of light is praised.
Because it goes upward and is the remedy for darkness, the giver is surely one who attains an upward path.
The gods are radiant, mighty and luminous, while rakshasas are of darkness; therefore a lamp is given.
By giving light a man becomes keen-sighted and endowed with brilliance. Having given them, he should not harm, steal or extinguish them.
The thief of a lamp becomes blind, goes into darkness, and is dull of life; the giver of a lamp shines in heaven garlanded with lamps.
Ghee is the first kind, and the second is plant oils; fat, marrow, bone and resin should not be used by one who desires well-being.
At a mountain precipice, in a thicket, at a shrine, at a crossroads, he should always give lamps who desires his own prosperity.
The giver of lamps, pure in soul, lights up his family and attains brilliance; he always reaches the same world as the luminaries.
I shall now tell of the offering of food to beings, the virtues and the fruits of the rite, for gods, yakshas, serpents, men, spirits and rakshasas.
Know that those brahmins in whose house gods, guests and children do not eat first are rakshasas, without the vashat call and without auspiciousness.
Therefore he should give the first portion, honoured, to the gods; and, bowing his head, he should offer the food-offering without sloth.
The household gods always expect it from the house, while the outside ones, the visitors, the other yakshas, rakshasas and serpents, expect it from outside.
Gods and ancestors live on what is given from here; pleased, they please these givers with life, fame and wealth.
He should offer food-offerings along with flowers to the gods; they should be with curds and drops, sacred, fragrant and pleasing to see.
For yakshas and rakshasas, offerings should be rich in blood and flesh, preceded by liquor and wine, adorned with parched grain and ointment.
Those dear to the nagas are always mixed with lotuses and water lilies; to spirits he should offer sesame with jaggery.
The giver of the first portion becomes the first to enjoy, endowed with strength and beauty; therefore he should give the first portion, honoured, to the gods.
The house of him who honours the household gods day after day shines; they should be worshipped by one who desires prosperity, giving the first portion with outstretched hands.
So Kavya, the descendant of Bhrigu, told this to the lord of the asuras; Manu told it to Suvarna, and Suvarna to Narada.
Narada told these virtues to me, O greatly radiant one. Knowing this, do you too practise it all, my son.
What is the fruit of giving incense and of lamps, and why do householders cast food-offerings?
[Bhishma] On this too they cite an ancient tale: the dialogue between Nahusha and Agastya and Bhrigu.
Nahusha, O great king, a royal sage of great austerity, attained the lordship of the gods through his good deeds here.
Even there, O king, Nahusha, dwelling in heaven, self-controlled, performed many kinds of rites, both human and divine.
All the human rites of that great soul, O king, continued in heaven, as did the eternal divine ones.
Fire rites, kindling sticks, kusha grass, flowers, food-offerings with parched grain, incense and lamp rites,
all of it went on in the house of that great-souled king; even in heaven he performed offerings of prayer and of mind.
That lord of the gods also worshipped the deities duly, all of them, in proper manner and as before, O scourge of foes.
Why, great sage, do we put up with this disrespect from this evil-minded Nahusha, lord of the gods?
[Agastya] How can I curse him, great sage? The boon-giver gave a boon to him, and you know it.
Whoever comes within my sight shall be in my power: the god was asked for this boon as he went to heaven.
Thus neither I nor you burned him, without doubt, and no other chief of sages cursed or felled him either.
Long ago, O lord, nectar was given him to drink, great soul that he is; for that reason we do not bring him down.
The god gave a boon that causes suffering to creatures; that vilest of men does unrighteous things to brahmins.
Tell us, best of speakers, what is to be done at this time, and we shall do as you say.
[Bhrigu] I have come at the Grandsire's command to counter Nahusha, who has taken up pride in his power.
Today that evil-minded lord of the gods will yoke you to his chariot; today I shall by my power make him unruly and no longer Indra.
Today, before your eyes, I shall set Shatakratu back as Indra, having dislodged from Indra's place that evil-minded sinner.
And today that vile lord of the gods, his mind struck by fate, will strike you with his foot, dull-witted, to his own ruin.
Enraged at his violence, I shall angrily curse that sinner, enemy of brahmins, who has strayed from dharma: "Become a serpent!"
Then that evil-minded one, his brilliance struck down by cries of "Shame!", I shall cast upon the earth as you watch, great sage.
That sinner, bewildered by sovereignty and strength, I shall treat, O sage, as it pleases you.
Thus addressed by Bhrigu, Agastya, the imperishable son of Mitra and Varuna, was greatly pleased, and his fever left him.
[Bhishma] While those two were speaking thus, all the rites of that great soul, divine and human, continued.
So too the lamp gifts, all the equipment, the food-offerings and every other kind of offering and observance of that great lord of the gods were all performed.
In the world of gods and the world of men, good conduct is praised by the wise. If these exist, O king, householders prosper, by gifts of incense, by lamps and by salutations.
As the first portion of cooked food is given to a brahmin, and offerings are made at the house's corner, the gods are thereby pleased.
As the householder's satisfaction arises from the food-offering, so the gods' pleasure becomes a hundredfold.
So the good praise the gift of incense and the gift of lamps, joined with salutations, as bringing virtue to oneself.
The rite a wise man performs with bathing and water, joined with salutation, pleases the gods; and all household deities, honoured by rule, are pleased.
Holding this view, King Nahusha, having gained great lordship over the gods, did this wondrous thing.
Then that lord of the gods fell away from the food-offering and did not duly perform the rule of incense, lamps and water. Then rakshasas disturbed the field of his sacrifice.
Then he summoned the best of sages, Agastya, to carry him, and Agastya, mighty, came swiftly from the banks of the Sarasvati, almost smiling.
Then the greatly radiant Bhrigu said to Mitra-Varuna's son: "Close your eyes, until I enter your matted hair."
As he stood like a post, the unfailing and greatly radiant Bhrigu entered his matted locks, to bring about the king's fall.
Then the lord of the gods came to that sage to be carried, and Agastya spoke to the lord of the gods, O lord of the people.
Yoke me quickly, Indra; to what place shall I carry you? Wherever you say, there I shall take you, lord of the gods.
So addressed, Nahusha yoked that sage; and Bhrigu, in his matted hair, was greatly delighted.
And Bhrigu, knowing the power of the boon, did not then show himself to the great-souled Nahusha.
Agastya did not grow angry, though yoked by Nahusha; but the king urged him with a goad, O Bharata.
That righteous one did not grow angry; but the lord of the gods, enraged, then struck Agastya on the head with his left foot.
When the head was struck, Bhrigu, within the matted hair, in great anger cursed Nahusha of sinful mind.
[Bhrigu] "Because in anger you have struck this great sage on the head with your foot, fall quickly to the earth, evil-minded one, having become a serpent."
So addressed by the unseen Bhrigu, he fell to earth as a serpent, O best of the Bharatas.
If Nahusha, O lord of the earth, had seen Bhrigu, he would not by his brilliance have been able to be felled.
By those various gifts, austerities and observances, even fallen, O great king, he kept his memory on earth; and he appeased Bhrigu, praying that the curse might end.
Then Agastya, moved by compassion, appeased Bhrigu for the end of the curse, O great king, and Bhrigu graciously granted it.
[Bhrigu] "A king named Yudhishthira will be born, the upholder of the Kurus; he will free you from the curse." Having said this, he vanished.
Agastya too, greatly radiant, having done Shatakratu's task, went to his own hermitage, honoured by the twice-born.
And you, O king, have raised Nahusha from that curse; he went to Brahma's abode as you watched, O lord of men.
Then, having felled Nahusha to the ground, Bhrigu went to Brahma's abode and reported it to Brahma.
Then the Grandsire, having summoned Shakra, said to the gods: "By my boon, gods, Nahusha obtained the kingship; enraged Agastya has cast him down to earth.
The gods can never carry on without a king; therefore let Shakra be consecrated again to the kingship of the gods."
As the Grandsire spoke so, O Partha, the gods, delighted, answered him, "So be it."
Consecrated by the blessed Brahma to the lordship of the gods, Vasava shone as before, O tiger among kings.
So did this happen of old through Nahusha's transgression; and Nahusha was again perfected by those same deeds.
Therefore lamps should be given by householders at dusk. The giver of lamps gains divine sight after death, and lamp-givers become radiant as the full moon.
For as many years as there are winks of the eye while a lamp burns, so many years the lamp-giver becomes handsome and wealthy.
[Bhishma] On this too they cite an ancient tale: the dialogue between a chandala and a degraded kshatriya, O Bharata.
[Kshatriya] You are aged, chandala, yet you behave like a child. You live in the dust of dogs and donkeys; why do you shrink from the dust of cows?
The act you do is censured by the good, and is a chandala's; why do you sprinkle in a pool of water what is spoiled by cow dust?
[Chandala] O king, long ago the dust of a brahmin's cows being driven along spoiled the soma, and the twice-born who drank that soma were harmed.
And that king, though consecrated, swiftly entered hell with all those priests, having lived on a brahmin's property.
Those too who there drank the milk, ghee and curds, brahmins together with kshatriyas, all entered hell.
Those cows, with their milk, killed sons and grandsons, and a couple, shaking, looking on at the cattle, lived righteously.
I lived there then, O king, a celibate student, master of my senses; my alms were spoiled by their dust, O lord of men.
Those who buy it, O king, and those who sell it, go to Raurava after reaching Vaivasvata, every one.
One who knowingly sells soma spoiled by dust, a learned brahmin turned usurer, perishes in a long night; having reached hell for thirty years, he lives on dog's dung.
Dog-like conduct, arrogance, and treachery toward a friend's wives: weighed in the scale, arrogance outweighs even dharma.
Look at me, a sinful dog, discoloured, fawn-coloured and lean, brought to this state through arrogance toward beings.
I was born in a wealthy family of great means, and in another birth, O lord, I had mastered knowledge and wisdom.
Knowing these faults, yet through pride and fury, I then ate the backs of living beings, their flesh.
By that conduct and that food I have reached this state; see the turning of time.
Look at me, covered in dust, running furiously, like a cloth-end set on fire, tormented as if by bees.
Householders cross over great sin by study of the Veda, and by gifts of many kinds, as the wise say.
So, O lord of the earth, the Vedic hymns carry across a brahmin who has done wrong, if he stands in an ashrama and is freed from all attachment.
But I was born in a sinful womb, best of kshatriyas; I find no certainty how I may be freed.
By some good deed of a former life I have memory of past births, and by it I wish to attain liberation, O king.
To me who have come to you, tell me, as I ask: how can I be freed from being a chandala, best of men?
[Kshatriya] Chandala, make a vow by which you will gain liberation: giving up your life for a brahmin, you will attain the goal you wish.
Giving your body to flesh-eaters in battle for a brahmin's sake, offering your life in the fire of war, you will be freed; you can be freed no other way.
[Bhishma] So addressed, O king, he offered his life at the front of battle for a brahmin's property, O scourge of foes, and attained the goal he desired.
Therefore, my son, you must guard a brahmin's property, O best of the Bharatas, if you wish for the eternal, highest goal, mighty-armed one.
[Bhishma] By their deeds, O Partha, men reach different worlds: the doers of good go to good worlds, the doers of evil to evil ones.
On this too they cite an ancient tale, dear child: the dialogue between the sage Gautama and Vasava.
There was a brahmin named Gautama, gentle, self-controlled and master of his senses. In a great forest he saw an elephant calf, motherless and wretched.
Seeing it, he, compassionate and firm in vows, kept it alive; and after a long time it grew very strong and large.
When that great elephant was in rut, the ichor flowing from it on all sides, Shakra, in the form of Dhritarashtra, seized the elephant.
Seeing it being carried off, Gautama of strict vows, the great ascetic, spoke to King Dhritarashtra.
Do not take my elephant, my son, raised with such pain, O ungrateful Dhritarashtra. They say friendship of the good comes at the seventh step; betrayal of a friend, O king, should never touch you.
He gave kindling and water, guarded the empty hermitage, was well-trained in the teacher's house and diligent in service to his teacher.
[Gautama] "Where the departed, doer of good, rejoices, and where the departed, doer of evil, grieves, in the abode of the great Vaivasvata, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "Those who are inactive, unbelievers, the faithless, sinners absorbed in sense objects reach Yama's torment; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "Vaivasvata's realm of the restraining of men, where no falsehood is spoken, where truth is, where the weak punish the strong, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "Those who live honouring their elder sister, father, mother and teacher, this world is for such, great sage; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "The Mandakini of King Vaishravana, of great enjoyments, open to those who enjoy, frequented by gandharvas, yakshas and apsarases, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "People devoted to guests, of good vows, who give lodging to brahmins, who eat what is left, sharing with their dependants, they too adorn the Mandakini."
[Gautama] "The beautiful forest on Meru's peak, richly flowering, frequented by the songs of kinnaras, where the broad Sudarshana rose-apple tree stands, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "Brahmins who are gentle, truthful, learned, delighting all beings, who study the Itihasa and Purana, and offer honey as oblation to the twice-born,
this world is for such, great sage; Dhritarashtra is not going there. If you know of a place that is known, tell it quickly, for I am going."
[Gautama] "The richly flowering, beloved forest of Narada, Nandana, resort of the king of kinnaras, home of gandharvas and apsarases, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "People skilled in dance and song, who always live together without begging, this world is for such, great sage; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "Where the lovely Uttara Kurus shine, rejoicing together with the gods, O king, where brahmins born of fire live, unborn of womb and born of mountains,
where Shakra rains down every desire, where women roam as they please, where no woman feels jealousy toward men, there I shall send you with this elephant."

[Dhritarashtra] "Those who have turned away from desire in all beings, who eat no meat, who have laid down the rod and wander, who harm neither the moving nor the unmoving, who are the self of all beings,
without hope, without possessiveness, free of passion, alike in gain and loss, in blame and praise, this world is for such, great sage; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "Beyond that shine the eternal worlds, of holy fragrance, stainless and free of sorrow, in the abode of the great King Soma, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "Those given to giving who never accept gifts, nor take wealth from others, to whom nothing is unfit to give to a worthy one, who are hospitable to all and of gracious mind,
those who forgive and do not speak ill of others though able, always of virtuous conduct, this world is for such, great sage; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "Beyond that shine eternal worlds, free of dust, free of darkness, free of sorrow, the great and well-ordered worlds of Aditya, there I shall send you with this elephant."

[Dhritarashtra] "Those devoted to study, intent on serving their teachers, ascetics of good vows, true to their word, who speak nothing against their teachers, always up and ready, doing their teacher's work at a word,
this world is for such, great sage, for the pure, of cultivated minds, established in truth, knowers of the Veda, great souls; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "Beyond those shine eternal worlds, of holy fragrance, stainless and free of sorrow, in the abode of the great King Varuna, there I shall send you with this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "Those who always sacrifice with the Chaturmasya rites, who obtain a thousand sacrifices of the sort, those faithful brahmins who offer the Agnihotra properly for three years,
great souls who bear the yoke of dharma with their own wives and stand rightly on the fitting path, the righteous who bear it, theirs is that goal; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "The worlds of Indra, free of dust and sorrow, hard to reach, desired by men, in that abode of great splendour, O king, I shall send this elephant.
The brave man who lives a hundred years, who studies the Veda, and the sacrificer who is heedful, all these go to Shakra's world; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "There are great worlds of Prajapati, on the back of heaven, free of sorrow, desired by those born in all worlds; there I shall send you with this elephant."

[Dhritarashtra] "Kings consecrated with the Rajasuya, righteous, protectors of the people, and those whose limbs are bathed in the closing bath of the Ashvamedha, theirs are those worlds; Dhritarashtra is not going there."
[Gautama] "Beyond that shine eternal worlds, of holy fragrance, free of dust and of sorrow; in that hard-to-reach and unassailable world of the cows I shall send this elephant."
[Dhritarashtra] "He who, owning a thousand cows, gives a hundred each year; who, owning a hundred, gives ten as he is able; who gives one from ten, or one from five, being given to charity,
and brahmins who grow old in celibacy and guard the speech of Brahman, wise and devoted to pilgrimage, they rejoice there in the aerial car of the cows.
Prabhasa, Manasa, the holy Pushkaras, the great lake, the holy Naimisha shrine, the Bahuda, the Karatoyini,
Gaya's Shiras of the cows, the Vipasha, the Sthulavaluka, the Tushni Ganga, the Dasha Ganga and the great lake,
the Gautami, Kaushiki and Paka, and the great-souled, firm in vows, who go to the Sarasvati, Drishadvati and Yamuna,
there they, of divine station, wearing divine garlands, auspicious, rich in holy fragrance, go on; Dhritarashtra is not there."
[Gautama] "Where there is no fear of cold and not the slightest fear of heat, neither hunger nor thirst, neither weariness nor sorrow, nor pleasure,
no one hated and no one dear, no kinsman and no enemy, neither old age nor death, neither merit nor sin,
in that pure and abundant realm, established in wisdom and goodness, in the holy abode of the Self-existent, my elephant will strive to go."
[Dhritarashtra] "Those freed from all attachments, of perfected selves and firm vows, established in the practice of spiritual yoga, go to the heaven goal.
Those pure ones attain here the holy abode of Brahman; Dhritarashtra, great sage, cannot be seen there by you."
[Vaishampayana] Agreeing "So be it," and having honoured Narada and taken his leave, the royal sage went to the city of Varanasi.
And by your service to your elders, O tiger among men, the king has been pleased, along with his servants, and so has the illustrious Gandhari.
[Vasudeva] Those by whom hundreds of kings and daityas were conquered, O Arjuna, when I no longer see them here, I live on, O Arjuna, hard to die.
The ancient sage, O descendant of Kuru, Parashara's son of great vows, of unfathomable mind, all-knowing, knower of the course of all deeds.
